That year depends on your mortgage rate, your rent, how fast the home gains value and what your invested cash earns. The defaults are a $400,000 home, $2,200 monthly rent and a 7.32% mortgage rate. With those inputs, the modeled break-even is year 21, and a 5% rate moves it to year 5. The rent vs buy calculator below compares your net worth if you buy with your net worth if you rent and invest the same cash. It also shows the year buying pulls ahead. In our internal modeling, we took a buyer who puts 20% down on the default $400,000 home and pays 3% in closing costs. That is $92,000 of cash on day one and a $320,000 loan. At 7.32% over 30 years, the principal and interest payment is $2,198.18 a month. Adding property tax, insurance and maintenance brings the first-month cost of owning to $3,032. A similar rental costs $2,215 a month with renter's insurance. The renter invests the $92,000 and the $817 monthly difference at a 6% return. Seven years in, buying leaves $169,338 and renting and investing leaves $210,495, so renting leads by $41,156. Share Interactive — edit any field How it works The calculator tracks two paths, buying and renting, month by month. Buying costs the down payment and closing costs on day one. Each month after that, the buyer pays the mortgage payment plus property tax, insurance and maintenance, each figured as a percent of the home's current value. HOA dues are added, and so is mortgage insurance at 0.5% of the original loan a year. Mortgage insurance applies only while the down payment is under 20% and the loan is above 80% of the price. Renting costs the rent, which grows each year, plus renter's insurance. The renter keeps the down payment and closing costs and invests them on day one. Each month, whichever path costs less invests the difference. At every year-end, buying net worth is the home value after selling costs, minus the loan balance, plus the buyer's own investments. Renting net worth is the renter's investments. The break-even year is the first year-end at which buying net worth is at least renting net worth. In our internal modeling, we compared buying with renting and investing the same cash over 1 to 30 years. We then changed one assumption at a time to see which ones move the break-even year. We wrote the model twice, once in Python and once in the calculator's TypeScript code, and the two versions agreed on every scenario below. You can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to check them. At the defaults, owning costs more than renting in the first month. The price-to-rent ratio, which is the price divided by 12 months of rent, is 15.2. Buying trails renting by $39,311 after 3 years. After 5 years, the gap is $40,669. After 7 years, it reaches $41,156. The gap then starts to close and is $39,815 after 10 years. After 15 years, buying is worth $346,033 and renting is worth $375,959. Renting is still ahead by $29,926 at that point. Buying first catches up in year 21, which is the break-even year at the defaults. Changing one input at a time shows which assumptions move the break-even year. At a 6% rate, the payment falls to $1,918.56 and the break-even comes in year 8. Renting is still ahead by $5,977 after 7 years. At 5%, the payment is $1,717.83 and the break-even is year 5. Buying is then ahead by $20,214 after 7 years. At 4%, the payment is $1,527.73 and the break-even is year 4. Buying leads by $45,917 after 7 years. Higher rent also helps buying. At $2,600 rent, a price-to-rent ratio of 12.8, the break-even is year 7. At $2,800 rent, a ratio of 11.9, it is year 5. Home price growth of 5% a year moves the break-even to year 5. At 1% growth, buying never catches up within 30 years. The investment return works in the other direction, because the renter invests the $817 monthly difference. At a 3% return, the break-even is year 9. At 9%, buying never catches up within 30 years. A smaller down payment pushes the break-even out. With 10% down, or $40,000, the cash to buy drops to $52,000. The principal and interest payment is $2,472.95, mortgage insurance is added on top, and the break-even moves to year 30. You can size your own down payment with our down payment calculator , and see how a monthly investment grows with our compound interest calculator . These results come from a model. They are not measurements, and they are not a forecast of home prices, rents or returns. The default mortgage rate comes from the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey . It is the 30-year fixed-rate average for the week of October 22, 2026. That average was 7.32%, down from 7.40% the week before. The other defaults are planning assumptions, and you should replace them with local figures. Property tax is set at 1.0%, insurance at 0.5% and maintenance at 1.0% of the home's value a year. Closing costs are 3%, selling costs are 6%, and home prices and rent each grow 3% a year. The investment return is 6%, and renter's insurance is $15 a month. Property tax and insurance vary a lot by state, so enter your own tax rate and insurance quote. For rent, use what a similar home rents for near you, and our guide on how much to spend on rent can help you set that budget. The model leaves out the income-tax effects of owning. Mortgage interest and property tax deductions help only filers who itemize, so find your bracket with our tax bracket calculator before you count on them. Moving costs and special assessments are not modeled either. To set a home price you can carry, run our mortgage affordability calculator first. Based on our internal modeling, buy only if you expect to stay past the break-even year. At the defaults, the break-even is year 21, so a seven-year stay favors renting and investing the difference. A lower mortgage rate, higher rent or faster home price growth moves the break-even earlier. The result swings back toward renting if home prices stall or your invested cash earns more than assumed. If you expect to move within a few years, the defaults favor renting for any stay shorter than the break-even year, so keep renting and invest the cash. If you want to buy for space, stability or control of the property, the model does not price those reasons. This calculator is informational and is not financial advice. Stock held more than one year gets the long-term rates. Those rates are 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on where the gain lands on top of your other taxable income. A gain on stock held one year or less is taxed as ordinary income. High earners also add the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax. The stock capital gains tax calculator below shows your gain, federal tax, surtax and proceeds after tax for 2026. In our internal calculation, we took a single filer with $85,000 of other taxable income. They sell stock bought for $30,000 for $50,000, which is a $20,000 gain. If they held it more than one year, the gain is taxed at 15%, so the tax is $3,000. If they held it one year or less, the same gain is taxed at 22% as ordinary income. That tax is $4,400. Holding past one year saves $1,400. Share Interactive — edit any field How it works The calculator starts with your gain, which is sale proceeds minus cost basis. Under IRS Topic 703 , your basis for stock is the purchase price plus commissions and recording or transfer fees. The calculator does not check basis. You also enter your filing status, your taxable income before this sale (after deductions) and your holding period. IRS Topic 409 treats stock held more than one year as long-term. In our internal calculation, we re-implemented the 2026 stacking rule in two separate programs. We ran the scenarios below through both to see how income and holding period change the tax. The two programs agreed on every scenario, and you can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to check them. Take a single filer with $20,000 of other taxable income and a $5,000 long-term gain. The whole gain sits inside the 0% bracket, so the tax is $0. To see the profit on a position before tax, use our stock profit calculator , and our guide to realized vs unrealized gains explains when a gain counts as realized. Long-term gains are stacked on top of your other taxable income. The part of the gain at or below the 0% limit is taxed at 0%. The part between the 0% limit and the 15% limit is taxed at 15%. Anything above the 15% limit is taxed at 20%. The limits come from Revenue Procedure 2025-32 . For single filers, the 0% bracket runs to $49,450 of taxable income. The 15% bracket runs to $545,500. Married couples filing jointly get limits of $98,900 and $613,700. Heads of household get $66,200 and $579,600. Married filing separately shares the $49,450 zero-rate limit but tops out at $306,850 for the 15% rate. At $85,000 of other taxable income, a single filer is already past the 0% limit. Every dollar of a $20,000 long-term gain then lands at 15%. A single filer with $40,000 of other taxable income and a $20,000 long-term gain lands in two brackets. The first $9,450 fills the rest of the 0% bracket. The other $10,550 is taxed at 15%, for a tax of $1,582.50. At $540,000 of other taxable income, a single filer's $30,000 gain crosses the top threshold. Of that gain, $5,500 is taxed at 15%. The remaining $24,500 is taxed at 20%, which brings the income tax to $5,725. The Net Investment Income Tax adds $1,140, for a total of $6,865. Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. The calculator figures the ordinary-income tax on your other taxable income plus the gain, then subtracts the tax on your other taxable income alone. For single filers in 2026, the 22% bracket ends at $105,700. The 24% bracket ends at $201,775. In the $85,000 case, income plus gain comes to $105,000. That total sits under $105,700, so the whole $20,000 is taxed at 22% for a tax of $4,400. A single filer with $100,000 of other taxable income and a $10,000 short-term gain crosses a bracket line. The first $5,700 of the gain is taxed at 22%. The other $4,300 is taxed at 24%, for a tax of $2,286. You can find your tax bracket or read how ordinary income vs capital gains tax differ. The Net Investment Income Tax is 3.8%, per IRS Topic 559 . It applies to the smaller of the gain or the amount by which modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is over a threshold. The threshold is $200,000 for single and head of household filers. It is $250,000 for married filing jointly and $125,000 for married filing separately. The calculator estimates MAGI as your taxable income plus the 2026 standard deduction plus the gain. That deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers. If you itemize, the estimate understates your MAGI. A single filer with $190,000 of other taxable income sells for a $40,000 long-term gain. Income tax on the gain is $6,000 at 15%. The surtax adds $1,520, for a total of $7,520. A married couple filing jointly with $650,000 of other taxable income and a $200,000 long-term gain pays 20% on all of it. That is $40,000 of income tax plus $7,600 of surtax, for a total of $47,600. The calculator covers federal tax for 2026 only. It leaves out state income tax, other investment income, qualified dividends, loss carryovers and wash sales, and it assumes the gain is your only investment income. If you live in a state with its own income tax, add the state figure on your own, because the calculator does not estimate it. The calculator is built for stock, exchange-traded fund (ETF) and fund shares in a taxable account. Sales inside a retirement account such as an individual retirement account (IRA) or 401(k) are not taxed this way. If you are selling real estate, use the rental property capital gains calculator . A loss owes no capital gains tax. A single filer who paid $30,000 and sells for $20,000 has a $10,000 loss. Topic 409 limits the net capital loss deduction to $3,000 a year, or $1,500 if married filing separately. Any excess carries forward. You report each sale on Form 8949 and summarize it on Schedule D (Form 1040). Hold a winning position for more than a year when you can. At $85,000 of other taxable income, a $20,000 gain costs $3,000 held long-term. Sold within a year, the same gain costs $4,400, a $1,400 difference in our internal calculation. A price drop larger than that $1,400 would cost more than the tax you save by waiting. If your other taxable income is under the 0% limit, long-term gains up to the room left in that bracket are tax-free. The calculator shows how much room you have. The 3.8% surtax adds to the bill only for high earners. State income tax, wash-sale or loss-carryover rules, or other investment income you did not enter can change this result. This calculator gives informational estimates rather than tax advice, and a preparer settles the individual case. Before you sell, enter your numbers in the stock capital gains tax calculator above and compare both holding periods. Frequently asked questions How is capital gains tax on stock calculated? Subtract your cost basis from the sale proceeds to get the gain. A long-term gain is stacked on top of your other taxable income and taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% by where it lands. A short-term gain is taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. High earners may also owe the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax. What are the long-term capital gains tax rates for 2026? The long-term rates are 0%, 15% and 20%. For single filers, the 0% rate covers taxable income up to $49,450. The 15% rate runs to $545,500, and 20% applies above that. Married couples filing jointly get limits of $98,900 and $613,700. How long do I have to hold a stock to get the long-term rate? Hold the stock more than one year, per IRS Topic 409, and the gain is long-term. Stock held one year or less produces a short-term gain, which is taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. Are short-term stock gains taxed at a higher rate? They can be, because short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. A single filer with $85,000 of other taxable income pays $4,400 on a $20,000 short-term gain. Held more than one year, the same gain costs $3,000. What is the Net Investment Income Tax on a stock sale? The Net Investment Income Tax is a 3.8% surtax described in IRS Topic 559. It applies to the smaller of your net investment income or your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) above a threshold. The threshold is $200,000 for single or head of household filers and $250,000 for joint filers. It is $125,000 if married filing separately. Can I owe no tax when I sell stock? Yes, if your long-term gain fits inside the 0% bracket. A single filer with $20,000 of other taxable income owes $0 on a $5,000 long-term gain. A sale at a loss also owes no capital gains tax. What happens if I sell stock at a loss? A loss owes no capital gains tax. Under IRS Topic 409, you can deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss a year, or $1,500 if married filing separately. Any excess carries forward. How do I find my cost basis? Your cost basis is usually the purchase price plus commissions and recording or transfer fees, per IRS Topic 703. Check your brokerage records for the price you paid and the fees charged. The calculator does not check basis, so the result depends on the figure you enter. mainEntity.name: Are short-term stock gains taxed at a higher rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can be, because short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. A single filer with $85,000 of other taxable income pays $4,400 on a $20,000 short-term gain. Held more than one year, the same gain costs $3,000.

mainEntity.name: What is the Net Investment Income Tax on a stock sale?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Net Investment Income Tax is a 3.8% surtax described in IRS Topic 559. It applies to the smaller of your net investment income or your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) above a threshold. The threshold is $200,000 for single or head of household filers and $250,000 for joint filers. It is $125,000 if married filing separately.

mainEntity.name: Can I owe no tax when I sell stock?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your long-term gain fits inside the 0% bracket. A single filer with $20,000 of other taxable income owes $0 on a $5,000 long-term gain. A sale at a loss also owes no capital gains tax.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I sell stock at a loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: A loss owes no capital gains tax. Under IRS Topic 409, you can deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss a year, or $1,500 if married filing separately. Any excess carries forward.

mainEntity.name: How do I find my cost basis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your cost basis is usually the purchase price plus commissions and recording or transfer fees, per IRS Topic 703. Check your brokerage records for the price you paid and the fees charged. The calculator does not check basis, so the result depends on the figure you enter.

But renting offers more flexibility and lower upfront costs, and it can be the better choice in high-price markets where monthly ownership costs far exceed rent for comparable properties. Renting vs Buying: Side-by-Side Renting Buying Upfront cost Low (first+last month, deposit ~$3–6k) High (3–20% down + 2–5% closing costs) Monthly cost Rent only (fixed term, may rise) Mortgage + taxes + insurance + maintenance Equity building None — money goes to landlord Yes — builds with each payment Flexibility to move High — relocate when lease ends Low — selling takes months + costs 6–10% Maintenance responsibility Landlord's (mostly) Owner's — budget 1% of home value/year Tax benefits None Mortgage interest + property tax deductions Break-even timeline N/A Depends on the mortgage rate and the price-to-rent ratio 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Rent when you plan to stay fewer than 5 years, value mobility, or live in a high-cost city where price-to-rent ratios are above 25x. Buy when you plan to stay 7+ years, have a stable income and emergency fund, and housing costs are reasonable relative to rent (price-to-rent ratio below 20x). The rent-vs-buy decision is more about your life stage than pure math. The true cost of buying a home Most people underestimate the true cost of homeownership. Beyond the mortgage payment, owners pay property taxes (typically 1–2% of home value per year), homeowner's insurance (~0.5–1%), HOA fees (if applicable), and maintenance — the standard rule is 1% of home value annually, but older homes can easily run 2–3%. On a $400,000 home with a 20% down payment, a 7% mortgage rate, 1.2% property tax, 0.8% insurance, and 1% maintenance, the true monthly cost is about $2,950 — before building any equity. After the equity portion, your actual 'rent equivalent' (the sunk cost) is closer to $2,200/month in the early years. The mortgage calculator and net worth calculator can help you model full ownership costs and how home equity builds your net worth over time. Why renting is not 'throwing money away' The most persistent myth in personal finance is that rent is wasted money. It's not — rent buys you housing, flexibility, freedom from maintenance, and the ability to deploy your down payment capital elsewhere. A $80,000 down payment invested in a diversified stock portfolio earning 8% annually grows to $860,000 over 30 years. That same $80,000 tied up as a down payment grows only as fast as home appreciation — historically 3–4% annually — reaching about $195,000 over 30 years. The gap closes when you factor in leverage (you control $400k of home with $80k), the forced savings effect of mortgage payments, and rent that would have otherwise exceeded mortgage costs. The math favors buying in low-to-moderate price markets and long holding periods. The price-to-rent ratio: your key metric The price-to-rent ratio is the clearest tool for the rent-vs-buy decision. Calculate it by dividing the home purchase price by the annual rent of a comparable property. A ratio below 15 favors buying when mortgage rates are low. A ratio of 15–20 is roughly neutral. Above 20, renting becomes increasingly competitive; above 25, renting usually wins financially. In 2024, San Francisco's price-to-rent ratio exceeds 40x — meaning a $1.5 million home rents for less than $40,000/year. Chicago and Cleveland run near 12–14x, clearly favoring buyers. Most U.S. metros fall between 15–25x. A practical non-obvious insight: the price-to-rent ratio also predicts your break-even point. A higher ratio pushes the break-even later, and a lower mortgage rate pulls it earlier. Rates move these numbers a lot: in our internal modeling, a $400,000 home renting for $2,200 (a ratio of 15.2) breaks even in year 5 at a 5% mortgage rate but in year 21 at 7.32%, which you can test in our rent vs buy calculator . When renting is the smarter financial move Renting is financially rational in several scenarios that many buyers overlook. When your job is unstable or you might relocate, selling a home within 2–3 years rarely recovers the 6–10% transaction costs (agent commissions, closing costs, repairs). You're often financially better renting and keeping capital flexible. Renting also makes sense during periods of elevated home prices and rates, when the monthly cost to own far exceeds rent. In many coastal markets in 2023–2024, buying required a 25–35% premium over renting comparable space — a drag that takes many years to overcome through appreciation. Renting in a high-rent area while house-hacking (buying a multi-unit property elsewhere and renting out units) is an increasingly popular strategy for building wealth without tying yourself to an expensive market. The rental property calculator can help evaluate investment property returns. If you rent, use the rental checklist of what to check before you sign and, for a first place, the first apartment checklist ; if you buy, start with the home buying checklist . Frequently asked questions Is renting or buying cheaper in 2024? In most U.S. markets in 2024, renting is cheaper on a monthly basis due to elevated home prices and 7%+ mortgage rates. However, buying builds equity while renting does not. The break-even point, when buying becomes the better financial deal, depends mainly on the mortgage rate and the price-to-rent ratio, and our rent vs buy calculator finds it for your numbers. How long should you own a home before selling? Financial planners generally recommend owning a home for at least 5–7 years before selling to recoup transaction costs (agent commissions, closing costs, repairs) through appreciation and equity buildup. Selling in fewer than 3 years often results in a net loss even in appreciating markets. What is the price-to-rent ratio? The price-to-rent ratio is the home purchase price divided by the annual rent of a comparable property. A ratio below 15 favors buying; above 20 favors renting. San Francisco exceeds 40x (strong rent signal); Cleveland runs near 12x (strong buy signal). Does renting build wealth? Renting itself doesn't build wealth — but investing the down payment and payment difference in the stock market can. In high price-to-rent ratio markets, renting and investing the capital often outperforms buying, especially over short-to-medium time horizons. semantic.text: ModernWallet Free Financial Calculators Calculators All calculators Auto Loan Mortgage Retirement Investing Portfolio Real Estate Net Worth Budget Tax Resolution Estate Planning Probate Elder Care Trump Account 529 College Savings Coast FIRE Business Loan Payoff Personal Loan Interest Per Day Taxable vs. Tax-Deferred Credit Card Payoff IUL Merchant Cash Advance Invoice Factoring Business Line of Credit PTO Cash-Out Zakat Life Insurance Needs Self-Employment Tax Operating Cash Flow Mileage Deduction Cash Conversion Cycle Freelance Rate HELOC S-Corp Tax Commercial Mortgage CD Calculator Emergency Fund Debt Consolidation Inflation Expense Ratio Social Security Break-Even Mileage Reimbursement Portfolio Rebalancing Hurricane Deductible Annuity Credit Card Interest Loan Payment HYSA vs CD Trump Account vs 529 Mortgage Recast Social Security COLA Roth vs Traditional 401(k) Florida Amendment 3 Student Loan Garnishment Tax Bracket Debt-to-Income Ratio Taxable Social Security Checklists Charitable Donation Deduction Car Loan Interest Deduction Rent vs Buy Stock Capital Gains Tax × ModernWallet / Compare / Ordinary Income vs Capital Gains Tax Ordinary Income vs Capital Gains Tax By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 28, 2026 Ordinary income is taxed at your regular federal rate, up to 37% in 2026. A long-term capital gain on that same money is taxed separately at 0%, 15%, or 20%. That's the distinction our calculators walk readers through when they're deciding when to sell an investment or how to take a bonus. The bucket a dollar falls into can matter more than how much of it you earn. Ordinary Income vs Capital Gains Tax: Side-by-Side Ordinary Income Capital Gains Tax What generates it Wages, salary, tips, self-employment income, interest, and gains on assets held 1 year or less Profit from selling a capital asset, like stock or real estate, held more than 1 year 2026 federal tax rates 7 brackets from 10% to 37%, based on total taxable income Just 3 rates: 0%, 15%, or 20%, based on total taxable income Holding period required None. The length of time you own something never matters More than 1 year (366 days or more) to qualify for the lower rate How it's reported Form W-2 or Schedule C, plus Schedule 1 for interest and other income Schedule D and Form 8949 Extra 3.8% investment-income surtax Never applies to wages directly. Can apply to interest and non-qualified dividends Applies once income tops $200,000 single / $250,000 married filing jointly Inside a traditional 401(k) or IRA Withdrawals are always taxed as ordinary income The lower rate never survives. Withdrawals come out taxed as ordinary income too Losses against the other type Capital losses offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year Losses offset capital gains dollar for dollar first, then up to $3,000 of ordinary income 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Lean toward treating a gain as long-term whenever you have a real choice about when to sell. Then let account type do the rest: pre-tax accounts for assets that throw off ordinary income, taxable accounts for long-term holdings and qualified dividends. That combination beats chasing either income type in isolation for most investors with more than a token amount at stake. Skip the strategy if you're a short-term trader who can't control holding periods, or if your investing already happens entirely inside a 401(k) or IRA. It's also not worth the effort when the amount involved is too small to justify the planning. Run your own numbers through ModernWallet's investing tools before you decide when to sell. What Counts as Ordinary Income Ordinary income is any money the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) taxes at your regular marginal rate, the same rate that applies to your paycheck. It covers wages, salary, tips, bonuses, and net income from a small business or freelance work. It also covers interest from a savings account or a CD, non-qualified dividends, and any gain on an asset you held for one year or less. Rent from a property you manage yourself falls into this bucket too, though depreciation can shrink the taxable amount. Withdrawals from a traditional 401(k) or a traditional individual retirement account (IRA) count as ordinary income as well, no matter what the money was invested in. Publication 525 lists the full range of taxable income types. What Counts as a Capital Gain A capital gain is the profit you make when you sell a capital asset for more than you paid for it. Stocks, bonds, mutual fund shares, real estate, and even a business you built and later sold all qualify as capital assets. The gain only becomes taxable once you actually sell, a rule called realization. You can watch a stock double in value and owe nothing in tax as long as you keep holding it, per the IRS guide to capital gains and losses. Sell it, and the profit gets classified one of two ways based entirely on how long you owned the asset first. That single detail, the holding period, decides whether the gain gets taxed like a paycheck or at a separate, lower rate built for long-term investors. Short-Term vs Long-Term Capital Gains Hold an asset for one year or less before selling, and the profit counts as a short-term capital gain, taxed at the same rate as your wages. Hold it for more than one year, and the profit becomes a long-term capital gain, taxed at the separate 0%, 15%, or 20% rate instead. The clock starts the day after you buy the asset and ends the day you sell it. If you bought on March 1, you have to wait until March 2 of the following year to sell and still qualify for the long-term rate. Selling on March 1 itself is one day too early. That single extra day carries real money. A single filer in the 32% bracket sells a stock position with a $15,000 gain one day short of the one-year mark. The IRS taxes that gain as ordinary income, for a $4,800 federal bill. Wait until day 366, and the same $15,000 gain drops into the 15% long-term rate for a $2,250 bill. That's a savings of $2,550 for changing nothing but the sale date. To see the tax on your own sale, enter your income, basis and holding period in our stock capital gains tax calculator . Ordinary Income vs Capital Gains Tax Rates for 2026 For 2026, ordinary income is taxed across seven brackets that run from 10% to 37%, and a long-term capital gain uses just three rates instead: 0%, 15%, or 20%. Both scales run off your total taxable income. The IRS fills the ordinary brackets first, then stacks any capital gain on top of that. That means wages can push a gain into a higher capital-gains bracket, even though the reverse never happens. Take a single filer with $90,000 of taxable income in the 22% ordinary bracket. An extra $10,000 in wages stays inside that same bracket, so the IRS taxes all of it at 22%, a $2,200 bill. The same $10,000 arriving as a long-term capital gain stacks on top of that $90,000 instead. It lands in the 15% bracket, since the wages already used up the $49,450 of 0% room, so the tax comes to $1,500. That's a $700 difference on the exact same $10,000, at the exact same income level. Nothing else about the filer changed. The gap widens further for anyone in a higher ordinary bracket, since the ordinary rate keeps climbing past 22% while the capital-gains rate tops out at 20%. High earners face one more wrinkle: a surtax that applies to investment income like this capital gain, but never to wages directly. The next section covers exactly when it kicks in. Where Qualified Dividends and the Net Investment Income Tax Fit In Qualified dividends get taxed at the same 0%, 15%, or 20% rate as a long-term capital gain, not at your ordinary rate. That preferential rate applies as long as you held the stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period surrounding the dividend's ex-dividend date. A dividend that fails that test is called a non-qualified dividend. It gets taxed at your regular marginal rate instead, per the IRS guide to dividends and other corporate distributions. Above certain income levels, both types of investment income can trigger the Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT), an extra 3.8% surtax on top of whatever rate already applies. It kicks in once your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) passes $200,000 for a single filer or $250,000 for a married couple filing jointly. The IRS has kept those two thresholds fixed since 2013, unlike most tax figures, rather than adjusting them yearly for inflation. Wages never trigger the NIIT directly, since it only applies to net investment income: interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income. A high earner instead pays a parallel 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above those same $200,000 and $250,000 thresholds. Both income types face an extra surtax past that line, just under different names. Add the NIIT to the earlier example, and a high earner's long-term capital gain can face 18.8% instead of 15%. Equivalent wages, meanwhile, face their ordinary bracket rate plus the 0.9% Medicare add-on. The two systems run more parallel than most people realize, but the capital-gains side still comes out lower in nearly every real bracket comparison. How a 401(k), IRA, or Roth Account Changes the Math A traditional 401(k) or traditional IRA erases the ordinary-versus-capital-gains distinction entirely, but not in your favor. Every dollar you pull out in retirement is taxed as ordinary income. That's true even if the account grew entirely from stock gains that would have qualified for the lower long-term rate in a regular brokerage account. A Roth IRA erases the same distinction the opposite way. Once you're 59 and a half, and the account has been open five years, every qualified withdrawal comes out completely tax-free. It no longer matters whether the growth inside came from contributions, dividends, or capital gains. Because of that, where you hold an asset can matter as much as what the asset is. Investments that throw off ordinary-taxed income, like bonds, real estate investment trusts (REITs), and actively traded funds, tend to do less damage inside a 401(k) or IRA. Stocks and funds you plan to hold for years already earn the lower capital-gains rate in a taxable account. They often keep more of that edge by staying in a regular brokerage account instead. One more wrinkle favors the taxable side. Assets you still own at death generally get a stepped-up cost basis, wiping out the capital gain for your heirs entirely. A traditional 401(k) or IRA gets no such reset, so heirs still owe ordinary income tax on every dollar they withdraw. Our 401(k) vs Roth IRA and Roth IRA vs Traditional IRA comparisons cover the contribution-side tradeoffs in more depth. Ways to Reduce the Tax You Owe on Either Type of Income Most of the tax you owe on either income type is controllable, through timing and account choice rather than the tax code itself. Hold winning positions past the one-year mark before selling. As the math above showed, moving a gain from short-term to long-term treatment alone can cut the tax bill by a third or more. Nothing about the investment itself has to change. Harvest losses against gains before December 31. Selling a losing position offsets a winning one dollar for dollar. Once losses exceed gains, up to $3,000 of the excess offsets ordinary income each year, with anything left over carried forward to future years. Sell into the 0% long-term rate during a low-income year. A gap year between jobs, a year funded mostly by savings, or the first year of retirement before Social Security starts can all create room to use it. That room sits under the $49,450 single or $98,900 married threshold, enough to realize a gain completely tax-free. Give appreciated stock directly to a charity instead of cash. You skip the capital-gains tax on the appreciation entirely, and if you itemize, you can still deduct the stock's full market value. That combination usually beats selling the stock and donating the after-tax proceeds instead. Put ordinary-income-generating assets inside a 401(k) or IRA, and keep long-term holdings in a taxable account, following the asset-location split covered above. An investor selling a rental property can also look at a 1031 exchange or opportunity zone fund to defer the gain instead of realizing it right away. Who This Approach Does Not Fit Active planning around this split fits an investor with real control over the timing of a sale and a gain worth the effort. It also assumes the investment sits in a taxable account, not a retirement account. It's not worth much attention if most of your investing already happens inside a 401(k) or IRA. None of these rates apply until you withdraw the money, and the withdrawal counts as ordinary income either way. It's also not worth chasing over a small gain. Saving a few percentage points on a $500 position is a few dollars, not an outcome worth planning around. Skip it if timing a sale around tax rates means holding an investment you no longer believe in, or missing money you genuinely need now. A stock you'd sell today for other reasons rarely becomes worth holding for a few more weeks just to save on taxes. It also doesn't apply to day traders or anyone running a pattern of frequent, short-term trades. Every gain in that pattern is short-term by definition, so there's no holding-period lever to pull, and loss harvesting and account location are the only real levers left. What Would Change This Answer Two changes would shift the guidance above. If Congress ever taxed long-term capital gains at the same rate as ordinary income, the entire incentive to hold past one year would disappear. Only the NIIT and loss-harvesting strategies above would still matter. The other is a bracket move on your end. Someone who expects to retire into the 0% long-term rate, with little other income, gets far more value from holding appreciated stock in a taxable account. Selling it slowly in retirement usually beats selling now to pay off debt or fund a big purchase. Model your own numbers with ModernWallet's capital gains tax calculator before you decide when to sell. Frequently asked questions What's the main difference between ordinary income and capital gains tax? Ordinary income, like wages and interest, is taxed at your regular marginal rate, which runs from 10% to 37% in 2026. A capital gain on an asset held more than one year gets taxed separately, at a flat 0%, 15%, or 20%. That's usually the lower of the two rates for the same amount of money. Are dividends taxed as ordinary income or capital gains? It depends on the dividend. A qualified dividend, paid on stock you've held for more than 60 days around the ex-dividend date, gets the same 0%, 15%, or 20% rate as a long-term capital gain. A non-qualified dividend gets taxed at your regular ordinary rate instead. What are the 2026 long-term capital gains tax brackets? For 2026, the 0% rate applies up to $49,450 of taxable income for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. The 15% rate covers the range above that up to $545,500 single or $613,700 married, and the 20% rate applies above those thresholds, per the IRS . Do capital losses offset ordinary income? Yes, but only up to $3,000 a year, or $1,500 if married filing separately. A capital loss first offsets any capital gains you realized that year, dollar for dollar. Only the leftover amount can reduce ordinary income, and anything beyond $3,000 carries forward to future tax years. Does selling exactly one year after buying count as long-term? No, the IRS requires you to hold the asset for more than one year, not exactly one year. If you bought on March 1, you must wait until March 2 of the next year to sell and qualify for the long-term rate. Selling on March 1 itself is one day too early and counts as short-term. How does the Net Investment Income Tax affect capital gains? The NIIT adds an extra 3.8% on top of your regular capital-gains rate once your MAGI passes $200,000 for a single filer or $250,000 for a married couple filing jointly. A long-term gain that would otherwise face a 15% rate effectively costs 18.8% once the NIIT applies, though it never applies to wages directly. What's the simplest way to see my own capital gains tax bill? Plug your purchase price, sale price, and holding period into ModernWallet's capital gains tax calculator to see the exact rate and dollar amount before you sell. Run the numbers before the trade, not after, so you can actually choose between selling now and waiting for the long-term rate. itemListElement.name: Ordinary Income vs Capital Gains Tax Rates for 2026

mainEntity.name: What's the main difference between ordinary income and capital gains tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ordinary income, like wages and interest, is taxed at your regular marginal rate, which runs from 10% to 37% in 2026. A capital gain on an asset held more than one year gets taxed separately, at a flat 0%, 15%, or 20%. That's usually the lower of the two rates for the same amount of money.

mainEntity.name: Are dividends taxed as ordinary income or capital gains?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the dividend. A qualified dividend, paid on stock you've held for more than 60 days around the ex-dividend date, gets the same 0%, 15%, or 20% rate as a long-term capital gain. A non-qualified dividend gets taxed at your regular ordinary rate instead.

mainEntity.name: What are the 2026 long-term capital gains tax brackets?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2026, the 0% rate applies up to $49,450 of taxable income for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. The 15% rate covers the range above that up to $545,500 single or $613,700 married, and the 20% rate applies above those thresholds, per the IRS.

mainEntity.name: Do capital losses offset ordinary income?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but only up to $3,000 a year, or $1,500 if married filing separately. A capital loss first offsets any capital gains you realized that year, dollar for dollar. Only the leftover amount can reduce ordinary income, and anything beyond $3,000 carries forward to future tax years.

mainEntity.name: Does selling exactly one year after buying count as long-term?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, the IRS requires you to hold the asset for more than one year, not exactly one year. If you bought on March 1, you must wait until March 2 of the next year to sell and qualify for the long-term rate. Selling on March 1 itself is one day too early and counts as short-term.

mainEntity.name: How does the Net Investment Income Tax affect capital gains?

acceptedAnswer.text: The NIIT adds an extra 3.8% on top of your regular capital-gains rate once your MAGI passes $200,000 for a single filer or $250,000 for a married couple filing jointly. A long-term gain that would otherwise face a 15% rate effectively costs 18.8% once the NIIT applies, though it never applies to wages directly.

mainEntity.name: What's the simplest way to see my own capital gains tax bill?

acceptedAnswer.text: Plug your purchase price, sale price, and holding period into ModernWallet's capital gains tax calculator to see the exact rate and dollar amount before you sell. Run the numbers before the trade, not after, so you can actually choose between selling now and waiting for the long-term rate.
